Definitions

Vocabulary is a finite set of elements denoted with VVV﻿. The elements w∈Vw \in Vw∈V﻿ are called words

A sentence is a finite list of words from a given VVV﻿, denoted as w1 w2 ... wnw_1 \ w_2 \ ... \ w_nw1​ w2​ ... wn​﻿

  • With V+V^+V+﻿ we denote the set of all sentences of any lenght over VVV﻿

A language model LLL﻿ over V+V^+V+﻿ is a function P:V+→RP: V^+ \rarr RP:V+→R﻿:

  • For any sentence s∈V+s \in V^+s∈V+﻿, we have P[s]≥0P[s] \ge 0P[s]≥0﻿
  • ∑s∈V+P[s]=1\sum _{s \in V^+} P[s] = 1∑s∈V+​P[s]=1﻿

Notation:

  • P[s]=P[w1 ... wn]P[s] = P[w_1 \ ...\ w_n]P[s]=P[w1​ ... wn​]﻿ is for a specific sentence (a number)
  • P(s)=P(w1 ... wn)P(s) = P(w_1 \ ... \ w_n)P(s)=P(w1​ ... wn​)﻿ is for a generic sentence (a function)

  • Product between TTT﻿ numbers → geometric mean of TTT﻿ numbers (inverse probabilities)
    • In this setting, the LM learn conditional probabilities over words (the first one conditioned on empty)
    • The inverse of the probability is a rough estimation of the number of choices the language model considered for the next word
      • If we think about P=1/NP = 1/NP=1/N﻿ (one word chose over all words considered equiprobable)

Perplexity: ”To what extent has the language model, on average, reduced the range of possible choices for the next word?” → Hence, the lower the perplexity, the better the language model.

  • The true perplexity of English is believed to be between 15 and 20
  • A deterministic language will have perplexity equal 1
  • In a uniform languge (not dependent on previous ones) P[wi]=P[w1∣...]=1/VP[w_i ] = P[w_1| ...] = 1/VP[wi​]=P[w1​∣...]=1/V﻿ → 1/V−TT=VT1/T=V\sqrt[T]{1/V^{-T}} = V^{T^{1/T}} = VT1/V−T​=VT1/T=V﻿

Shannon proposed the concept of entropy to measure the information content of a probability distribution

  • very rare event carries a lot of information, while common ones doesn’t

Suppose XXX﻿ is a discrete random variable over X\mathcal{X}X﻿ with probability distribution P(x)P(x)P(x)﻿. The information content of x∈Xx ∈ Xx∈X﻿, denoted I[x]I[x]I[x]﻿, is defined as:

  • if the base is two the information is measured in bits, if it is eee﻿ in nats (natural digits)

The I[x]I[x]I[x]﻿ is like a transformation of a random variable

  • It makes sense to define

    E[I[x]]=E[−log⁡P[x]]=−∑x∈XP[x]log⁡P[x]=H(P)=H(x)E[I[x]] = E[-\log P[x]] = - \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P[x] \log P[x] = H(P) = H(x)E[I[x]]=E[−logP[x]]=−∑x∈X​P[x]logP[x]=H(P)=H(x)﻿

Properties of entropy

  • 0≤H(P)≤log⁡∣X∣0 \le H(P) \le \log |\mathcal{X}|0≤H(P)≤log∣X∣﻿
  • H(P)=0  iff  P=1  for some  x∈XH(P) = 0 \;\text{iff}\; P= 1 \;\text{for some}\; x \in \mathcal{X}H(P)=0iffP=1for somex∈X﻿ (thus all the others zero)
  • H(P)=log⁡∣X∣  iff  P=1∣X∣  for all  x∈XH(P) = \log |\mathcal{X}| \;\text{iff}\; P= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}|} \;\text{for all}\; x \in \mathcal{X}H(P)=log∣X∣iffP=∣X∣1​for allx∈X﻿

The information we get by using QQQ﻿ instead of PPP﻿ is called cross entropy

  • We cannot swap the two
  • Higher the difference between the two distributions bigger is the cross entropy

We define the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence on P,QP, QP,Q﻿ distributions over X\mathcal{X}X﻿

  • Gibbs’s Inequality DKL(P∣∣Q)≥0D_{KL}(P||Q) \ge 0 DKL​(P∣∣Q)≥0﻿ and equal only if the two are equal

  1. Stationarity: when the probability of seeing a word in the seqence doesn’t depend on its position
  1. Ergodicity: everything that can be generated from non-zero probability is generated
